faq.answer: No. Confidentiality, mentorship, shared expertise, crisis, therapy, safety, or a rare opportunity may explain a deep conversation. Compare repeated choices with consent and power matched.
faq.question: Does one intense conversation prove one-to-one Type Five?

faq.answer: A supervisor, therapist, mentor, partner, or gatekeeper changes what can safely be disclosed. Consent and the ability to leave determine whether selectivity reflects choice or constraint.
faq.question: Why must power and consent be part of the comparison?

faq.answer: Comparable depth across several safe relationships, transparent group support, easy changes of confidant, and comfortable refusal of intensity should reduce confidence in the subtype account.
faq.question: What counterexample weakens the focused-trust hypothesis?

sections.body_md: Within a Type Five hypothesis, one-to-one may emphasize opening substantial thought or feeling through a carefully chosen relationship. Selectivity is an observation to compare, not proof of hidden intensity or a fixed bond style.
sections.title: Describe focused trust as a secondary hypothesis

sections.body_md: Use two similarly private topics and compare a trusted peer with another safe person after matching confidentiality, consent, power, and time known. Ask what changes when the same person controls pace and can decline.
sections.title: Compare disclosure with equal consent and power

sections.body_md: The one-to-one label organizes observations about focused trust and disclosure; it is not evidence about bodily mechanisms, neurological wiring, attraction biology, or an innate pairing system.
sections.title: Reject biological or neurological explanations

sections.body_md: A person may be socially warm, maintain several close relationships, or share little in an intense conversation. Breadth and depth can coexist, so neither exclusivity nor visible intensity is required.
sections.title: Allow broad warmth and ordinary boundaries

sections.body_md: Therapy, supervision, mentorship, research collaboration, minority safety, trauma history, family privacy, cultural etiquette, and unequal power can all narrow disclosure to one person. Consent must remain revocable.
sections.title: Audit confidentiality, mentorship, and safety

sections.body_md: Confidence should fall when the person shares comparable depth across several safe relationships, uses transparent group support, changes confidants without identity threat, or declines intensity while preserving trust.
sections.title: Use safe plural relationships as a challenge

sections.body_md: A single instrument and sample cannot establish universal subtype ontology or cross-cultural equivalence. This hypothesis cannot predict compatibility, loyalty, intimacy, or relationship outcomes.
sections.title: Keep trust language local and non-predictive

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: Across five days, select two private conversations and one group-support event with different relationship roles.

Observable signal: Record confidentiality, invitation, consent, power difference, time known, topic depth, pace control, and ability to stop.

Page-specific signal: Compare similarly private topics only after safety, consent, and power are matched as closely as possible.

Alternative explanation: Check mentorship, therapy, shared expertise, attachment norms, family privacy, culture, trauma safety, and role duty.

Reflection prompt: Identify one plural or group relationship that supports depth and use it to test the focused-trust hypothesis.

seo.description: Type Five one-to-one is a traditional subtype hypothesis about selective deep disclosure, focused trust, and exchanging an inner world with a particular person. Intense conversation, mentorship, confidentiality, or a small circle does not establish subtype because safety, attachment norms, role boundaries, consent, power, and shared expertise may shape the same pattern.
seo.title: Type Five one-to-one: a selective depth and trusted disclosure hypothesis
